items.title: Charanjit Singh
items.author: Flow State
items.content: It’s Friday so we’re listening to something more upbeat. Today we’re listening to Charanjit Singh, an Indian composer and electronic musician from Bombay. Earlier this week Synthesizing: Ten Ragas to a Disco Beat. He was born in 1940, his parents instrument makers, and he played many different instruments growing up. His versatility earned him plenty of gigs in Bollywood as a session player, though by the early 1980s he’d grown bored of the formula. Around that time, the Japanese corporation Roland released the TB-303 bass synthesizer and TR-808 drum machine. Singh was attracted to these newfangled devices as a way to pursue a new musical direction. He used them, along with the Jupiter 8 synthesizer, to make Ten Ragas to a Disco Beat, which was released in 1982 to little fanfare. Decades later, the album was rediscovered and recognized as an incredibly prescient realization of electronic dance music, especially its acid house-style use of the 303. The record was recently reissued by the label Light in the Attic. A few years before Singh passed away in 2015, he told of the Roland and Jupiter instruments, “At home I practised with the combination and I thought ‘It sounds good – why not record it.’”

items.title: The Sweet Enoughs
items.author: Flow State
items.content: Today we’re listening to The Sweet Enoughs, an Australian trio led by bassist Paul Bender. He started the group in the late 2010s along with his Hiatus Kaiyote bandmate Simon Mavin (keys) and Lachlan Mitchell (guitar). The group’s first record was 2020’s , a sort of easy listening / exotica themed record that we’ve excerpted on many mixes. Their new record, Another Helping of the Sweet Enoughs, plays a similar style, channeling mid-century composers like Les Baxter and Piero Umiliani. The record was executive produced by the fictional Greek yacht-faring maestro Yannis Dreamlake, who gives an exclusive interview that accompanies the album’s Bandcamp release.

items.title: Across the Horizon Ep. 72: Marisa Anderson & Alan Sparhawk
items.author: Flow State
items.content:
On today’s episode of Across the Horizon, Bob Holmes of the band SUSS has a conversation with and Alan Sparhawk (formerly of Low). Marisa and Alan are two of the major curators for Vol.1 and Vol. 2 of the Across the Horizon music series and they discuss their contributions as well as those from Liz Draper, Charlie Parr, Kenneth Gregory, and EDT. The transcript of this discussion was originally published as an article on Talkhouse.

For Flow State, we’ve featured Anderson’s music a few times before (worth listening to if you haven’t heard it), so we’re playing records by artists mentioned on the episode. First up is portal iii’s self-titled album from 2020, a post-rock ambient record by Liz Draper (bass), Chris Gray (drums), and Charlie Parr (guitar). Second we’re playing by Liz Draper, from 2025, which similarly uses silence to punctuate its spare instrumentation.

items.title: Flow State Episode 347
items.author: Flow State
items.content:
Today’s mix opens with a new ambient track by Líom, followed by a dub ambient track by Acid Springfield. There are two ambient/field recording pieces, one by Ben Seretan and the other by Saapato. We play a favorite composition by the late Daniel Lentz (h/t Evan). Then more new ambient music by Windy & Carl with Optigan Conservatory, Dream Crease, and Emily A. Sprague. We play a favorite cue from Ari Balouzian’s new score for the movie . Then a vinyl rip of Erik Hall’s performance of with the Metropolis Ensemble. The pace picks up with Stella Z, Cousin, and Lake People. A house track from Aparde concludes the mix. We hope you enjoy.

items.title: Windy & Carl
items.author: Flow State
items.content:
Today we’re listening to Windy & Carl, an American space rock duo consisting of Windy Weber and Carl Hultgren. We recommended the husband and wife pair for the first time last year. Windy & Carl came up in the Michigan indie/experimental scene in the ‘90s by applying many effects to guitars, creating shoegaze-adjacent ambient pieces. They just released a new LP, Windy&Carl Meet Optigan Conservatory, in September. It’s a collaboration with their longtime friends Frank Rotondo and Fred Thomas, who contribute electric keyboard and synths over the guitars in largely improvised sessions. We’re also playing , which was originally self-released in 1994 and is being reissued by Kranky; that one showcases their early experimentation with stretching, distorting, modulating, and looping guitar sounds.

We wish you a great start to your week.

items.title: Cousin
items.author: Flow State
items.content: It’s Friday so we’re listening to something more upbeat. Today we’re listening to Cousin, an Australian electronic musician from Sydney. His first instrument was the recorder, which he was taught in primary school; that led to “the clarinet, then to the saxophone, bass guitar, and guitar, all with some casual tutelage on drums from his dad,” according to a Mixmag profile. He began to DJ and produce electronic music, and in his digital compositions he creates very naturalistic sounds and impressive acoustics. We’re playing two of his albums:

items.title: Heathered Pearls (Interview)
items.author: Flow State
items.content:
Today we’re listening to Heathered Pearls, a Polish-American electronic musician based in Brooklyn. He was born in Częstochowa and moved to Michigan with his parents as a kid, growing up in the Detroit exurbs. He gravitated toward beatless electronic music, but also found influences in the local Detroit scene – from which he highlights two memorable tracks below. Jakub Alexander started the project Heathered Pearls to collect ambient electronic music that are minimal in style, with focused attention on the details of the synth loops, their effects, and interplay. “When I make music,” he told us, “I think of it as the prettier side of the noise scene.” We’re first playing his new album, , which came out in March, followed by his 2012 LP, , which is more atmospheric. A conversation with Jakub follows the streaming links.

What’s your earliest memory of music?

Watching my mom and her friends up late at night listening to The Police’s through the cracked open door.

How were you first introduced to ambient music?

In the early mid-90s, Deep Forest, Enigma, and Orbital were probably the firestarters. I wanted more of the beatless moments, so I went down a few different avenues and found trance and local Detroit dub, which were enough subgenres, but they opened up a can of worms for me. 

What early listening most influenced the direction of your sound?

For Heathered Pearls specifically, which was the aughts, so probably just what I have had listed for years on my Facebook in 2010: Gas, Casino Versus Japan, High Wolf, Dettinger, Maurizio, Markus Guentner, burger/ink, Lawrence, Kaito.

What acts / tracks in the Michigan scene inspired you the most and stick with you to this day?

This Juno track my friend Danny Scales played for me when we lived together.

And this Underground Resistance cut:

Both together, I think, marry the spectrum of music I make but come from different sides of the sound that comes from Michigan’s scene.

As Heathered Pearls, you’ve oscillated between ambient and more four-on-the-floor music. Tell us about that journey, and maybe some of the similarities or differences between those production modes.

I wish I could make music for the dance floor; when I make music, I think of it as the prettier side of the noise scene. If I were talented enough, I’d just make IDM. I’m not a piano player; I can’t strum a guitar, keep a beat on a drum kit, or have the balls to write lyrics, but if you leave me with your melody and let me affect it, then I feel at home.

You’ve also been on the other side of the table as an A&R. Tell us how you approached that job, how you assessed demos and such. Did that experience affect you as a musician at all?

Rarely do I sign a lot of the music that aligns with the lane of music that I make. I think I do my job really well because I can relate to everyone involved. I’ve made myself do the work that some people find boring or shitty, and I’ve seen enough outcomes in so many different scenarios in the last 30 years that it gives me more compassion than most. If it’s in the studio, before a show, over dinner, or just a phone call, I feel like I understand it better than most when people start asking the tougher questions. Listening to the music is the fun part.

What was your studio setup for ? What instruments/gear/software did you use to make the record?

Reason and no samples. I know it’s not the prettiest answer or the answer that you might’ve wanted to read, but I try to push what the program comes with to make it my own.

How do you discover new music these days? Any recent notable finds?

YouTube still. I’ve recently been on a newer jazz kick, sitting on a lot of trip-hop I found over the last few years, and I like what the kids are doing with shoegaze.

Name an underrated artist from the past 50 years.

What are you working on next?

I’ve been dealing with dizziness for a couple years now, which has kind of shrunk my world a bit if anyone out there also battles with it. This sort of hinders the part of me that can make ambient music, since I find most sounds like what I wanna put out, but I’m feeling slightly better very recently. I hope to make a few more singles or an EP next year and then eventually another album which I’ve already sort of collected the influences which is a process that I love to do before making new music.
